data.title: Middle East Eye: Analysis: The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Analysis: The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
The trauma of the Hamas-led 7 October attack may have bypassed the Haredi spiritual leadership and its veteran MPs, but the wider Haredi public, including the generally more conservative Lithuanian community, understands that something momentous has happened in Israel. This is particularly true of the younger generation.

data.author: Shahir Shahidsaless

The US president can choose not to start another all-out conflict - but he cannot keep Tehran bleeding indefinitely
An Iranian woman holds up a portrait of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in front of an anti-Trump billboard in Tehran, on 3 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off
On Monday, US President Donald Trump appeared to rule out another major offensive against Iran, at least for now. After speaking with Qatar’s prime minister, he said Washington was maintaining the “status quo”.
In a Truth Social post, he said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait favoured continuing the naval blockade and “Operation Iron Gate”. Further escalation was “quite unlikely”, he suggested, although US forces remained “locked and loaded”.
Days earlier, Trump had been considering new strikes. Now he appears to favour keeping Iran under economic and military pressure without risking another major war.
The flaw is obvious: Washington can choose to maintain a blockade. It cannot decide how long Tehran will tolerate it.
Also on Monday, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called Washington a “desperate gambler”, denounced reports of “imaginary talks”, and demanded that the US “surrender” to Iran’s conditions.
Trump sees a manageable stalemate; Tehran sees an unacceptable siege.
For the Islamic Republic, this confrontation is existential. An indefinite blockade would inflict mounting economic damage, without guaranteeing relief or protection from another attack. Meanwhile, Gulf producers continue selling whatever oil they can export. Iran is left bleeding while others continue business.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UN chief tells Turkey climate summit: 'This is the path to mutually assured destruction'
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
UN chief tells Turkey climate summit: 'This is the path to mutually assured destruction'
“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres told world leaders at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Wednesday.
The UN chief said that the slow international response to the climate crisis had put the world on this path, and that rapid action was needed to avert it.
His comments set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders at the UN conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, Reuters reported.
Guterres pointed to rising carbon emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters in his speech.
“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs.”
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.
The summit opened on Monday and has, relative to its importance, received little attention against a backdrop of numerous wars, rampant inflation and other crises.
Rapidly rising global temperatures feed into these other crises, driving conflict and competition for resources. Oil and gas companies have profited hugely from the war on Iran, which has driven up the price of fossil fuels.

Off
Noura Sheikh al-Eid bid farewell to her husband and daughter as they left Gaza for medical treatment in Egypt.
It was meant to be a temporary goodbye.
But as the 54-year-old Palestinian mother returned from the departure station to her displacement tent on 5 November, an Israeli sniper shot and killed her.
“We are in shock,” Mohammed Sheikh al-Eid, Noura’s brother, told Middle East Eye.
“I lost my 14-year-old son during the famine, while he was trying to get aid. I swear to God, I did not grieve for him the way I have grieved for my sister,” he said.
“I considered her my second mother because she was the one who raised me.”
Since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, Israeli forces have repeatedly opened fire on Palestinians near the so-called "yellow line", which marks the boundary of areas under Israeli military control in Gaza.
Residents face indiscriminate gunfire from Israeli soldiers, military vehicles, lifters and quadcopters, including in areas beyond the line where civilians attempt to go about their daily lives.

The night before Noura was killed, relatives gathered at their tent in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, to bid farewell to her husband, Atallah Abu Athra, and their daughter, Hiba Abu Athra.
“Her husband suffers from heart disease and diabetes, and his condition has deteriorated to the point where he developed gangrene,” Sheikh al-Eid said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: A journey down Egypt's Red Sea coast to find Sufi saints and a mystical lyre
data.author: Sean Mathews
data.summary:
A journey down Egypt's Red Sea coast to find Sufi saints and a mystical lyre
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Mon, 11/09/2026 - 10:44
El-Quseir once welcomed explorers, warriors and Hajj pilgrims, but today its bypassed in favor of bigger Red Sea resorts
El-Quseir is filled with crumbling Ottoman-era houses with protruding wooden balconies (MEE/Sean Mathews)
Off
El-Quseir is pitch black at night. The only light inside this decaying labyrinth of a port comes when a battered Bajaj motorcycle purrs down the odd alley, casting a headlight on one of the town’s many stray dogs, or a passerby flashes a phone, lighting up a decaying wooden balcony.
The old mayor’s house is easy to find in the darkness. It emits a warm, golden light. When I arrive, a crowd is already gathered on the colonnaded veranda; some men in djellabas, others in the uniform skinny jeans of the Middle East.
I spot the odd Cairo hipster among them. The women attendees are especially radiant in make-up. Why shouldn’t they be.
Tonight is a Hazz night, the name, which in Arabic means luck, given to soirees down Egypt’s Red Sea coast, where the simsimiyya , a triangular lyre, is played to ballads about old ports, friendships and legendary seafarers.
The simsimiyya looms large over El-Quseir.
“The men here would be at sea for four months at a time. They would save a spot on their dhow just for a simsimiyya player to entertain them,” Aly El-Sayed, the founder of Bahar, a community organisation working to preserve the city's heritage and marine ecosystem, told me.
Aly is the host of tonight’s gathering. The old mayor’s house, a butter-yellow bungalow built in 1888, has been repurposed as Bahar’s home.
“We tried not to change much. We were even careful not to paint too much,” El-Sayed said.
'They sang all the time'
I knew that music was central to life aboard dhows, traditional wooden sailing boats, that plied goods, including slaves, between East Africa and Arabia up until the mid-20th century.

Open letter challenges Jewish community body over its denunciation of Green Party and response to Israel’s actions against Palestinians
Members of the Jewish Bloc for Palestine take part in a Free Gaza protest, near Admiralty Arch in central London, on 1 May 1 2024 (Adrian Dennis/AFP)
Off
Hundreds of British Jews have accused the Board of Deputies of British Jews of “genocide denial” in an open letter condemning its decision to declare the Green Party racist over its stance on Zionism.
The letter, released on Tuesday by Jews Against Genocide Denial, accuses the prominent Jewish representative organisation of shielding Israel from accountability and silencing criticism within its own ranks.
Historian Avi Shlaim, former South African MP and arms trade campaigner Andrew Feinstein, and human rights lawyer Margaret Owen are among the more than 250 signatories listed in the document.
The intervention follows the board’s decision on 25 October to declare that the Green Party of England and Wales had become a racist party after adopting a conference motion treating Zionism as a form of racism.
The board’s resolution, passed by 118 votes to one, argued that the Green policy stigmatised a connection to Israel that forms part of many British Jews’ religious, cultural and national identity.
The letter’s signatories rejected that interpretation, while stressing that they did not all share the same view of the Green motion’s merits.
“Some Jewish Greens supported it, some opposed it, some thought it unnecessary, given the party’s already strong stance against Israel’s oppressive regime and war crimes,” they wrote.

data.summary:
Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/11/2026 - 11:17
Mansour Abbas says the prime minister's speech vilifying Palestinian parties put him at risk
Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks on during a speech on the opening day of the new Israeli parliament in Jerusalem on 10 November 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off
The leader of the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said on Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held private talks with him through a close associate, despite publicly branding Palestinian parties "terror supporters who hate Israel".
"He was interested in our position on the law barring an indicted lawmaker from serving as prime minister, and whether we really intended to enter a coalition and replace Netanyahu's government," Abbas told Kan public radio.
"When it serves his interests, Arab citizens suddenly become legitimate, he becomes 'Abu Yair', and Mansour Abbas becomes a worthy partner in his eyes."
The Palestinian-led United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List won a record 19 seats combined, following a surge in turnout among Palestinian voters in Israel, giving them the balance of power.
In a speech to parliament on Tuesday evening, Netanyahu said the United Arab List and the Joint List were seeking to end Israel’s existence, adding that the two parties disagreed only on "what kind of state will arise on its ruins".
"What is the true goal of these factions?" Netanyahu said. "Is it only to improve the socioeconomic conditions of Arab citizens in Israel? We have no problem with that. But that is not their real goal."
Addressing those considering forming a government with Palestinian parties, Netanyahu added: "Don't you understand what they really want to achieve? What their national aspiration is?"

data.title: Middle East Eye: Egypt deployed forces to Saudi Arabia before Sisi's public pledge of military support, sources say
data.author: MEE correspondent
data.summary:
Egypt deployed forces to Saudi Arabia before Sisi's public pledge of military support, sources say
Submitted by
MEE correspondent
on
Wed, 11/11/2026 - 11:10
Egypt sent troops, Rafale fighter jets, helicopters and transport aircraft to the kingdom despite major disagreements within the military's top brass over Cairo's role in the conflict
Egyptian army special forces can be seen in northern Sinai province on 20 October 2023 (Kerolos Salah/AFP)
On
Egypt deployed forces and military aircraft to Saudi Arabia and moved air defence systems to strategic locations across the country long before President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi publicly pledged Cairo's support for Riyadh, Egyptian military sources have told Middle East Eye.
The deployment included a squadron of Rafale fighter jets, eight helicopters and four large transport aircraft, an Egyptian military source said on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to speak with the media.
Egyptian naval warships had also moved towards the southern Red Sea, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, the source added.
The reported naval movements came amid growing Egyptian concern over the security of Red Sea shipping lanes and the threat posed by Houthi attacks in Yemen.
In August, Egypt reportedly increased its naval presence near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, with reports claiming that modern frigates and corvettes had been deployed towards the southern entrance of the Red Sea.
Separately, Al Jazeera Arabic's open-source investigations unit reported last month that flight-tracking data had identified two Egyptian military C-130 Hercules transport aircraft operating in Saudi airspace.
The aircraft, identified by their registration numbers SU-BAI and SU-BEW, were tracked over western Saudi Arabia before their signals disappeared.

data.title: Middle East Eye: HSBC 'sharia-compliant' fund to exclude arms companies after Israeli-linked revenue exposed
data.author: Imran Mulla
data.summary:
HSBC 'sharia-compliant' fund to exclude arms companies after Israeli-linked revenue exposed
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Wed, 11/11/2026 - 10:11
Move comes after MEE revealed HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund purchased shares in world’s second-largest arms company
A branch of HSBC bank on a street in central London on 27 October 2026 (AFP)
Off
The UK’s largest “sharia-compliant” fund is divesting from companies which take more than 5 percent of their revenue from weaponry, after Middle East Eye revealed last month that it purchased more than $100m worth of shares in companies linked to the Israeli military in the first half of this year.
The new change means the British banking giant HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund is expected to divest from major companies including RTX, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell International, BAE Systems and Palantir.
The HSBC fund began tracking the S&P Global 1200 Shariah Select Index, a benchmark of companies screened for compliance with Islamic finance principles, in March. The fund is passively managed, which means it mirrors the index's investments.
In early November, the index updated its methodology and is set to implement the changes on 23 November. It will now exclude defence and weapons companies, military contractors and related sectors from the index.
According to the new criteria, the index will exclude companies with a more than 5 percent exposure to military contracting, nuclear weapons, depleted uranium, incendiary weapons, biological weapons and small arms, among other types of weaponry.
According to most screening guidelines, businesses can be deemed “sharia-compliant” if less than 5 percent of their income derives from sources categorised as impermissible.
The index did not previously exclude companies with exposure to most types of weaponry.
The HSBC fund is overseen by a board of Islamic scholars.
